analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy law to cover teens and bans targeted ads aimed at kids online.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill unanimously on March 5, 2026, but the House has taken no vote since receiving it, leaving it parked at the desk.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill updates the 1998 children's online privacy law. It extends protections to teenagers age 13 to 16, not just children under 13. It bans using a child's or teen's personal data to target ads at them individually, limits what data websites and apps can collect, and gives parents and teens the right to see, correct, and delete that data. It also requires reasonable security for the data and lets the FTC and state attorneys general enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 13 and teens 13 to 16, and their parents. They get a legal right to have a platform explain what data it holds, delete it, and correct errors; a ban on individual-targeted advertising built from their personal information; limits on data collection beyond what a service needs; notice before their data is stored abroad; and required security safeguards. State attorneys general can sue on their behalf.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act to 'teens,' defined as individuals age 13 through 16, who previously had no federal online privacy protections beyond the under-13 rules.

It makes it unlawful to collect, use, or share a child's or teen's personal information for individual-specific advertising — ads targeted to a specific kid based on their personal data, profiling, or a device identifier — with exceptions for contextual ads and ads the user asked for.

Parents and teens gain the right to a description of the data collected, the ability to delete it or refuse further collection, the ability to challenge and correct inaccurate information, and to obtain a copy of it; operators must also maintain reasonable security practices for children's and teens' data.

Operators may not collect more personal information than is consistent with the service a child or teen requested, may not retain it longer than reasonably necessary, and must notify parents or teens before storing or transferring the data outside the United States.
Both the FTC and state attorneys general can enforce the new rules, and the bill lets states enact stronger protections of their own, preempting state law only where it conflicts with this act.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial websites, apps, and online platforms — especially social media, gaming, and anything ad-supported — bear the cost of re-engineering data practices, honoring deletion requests, and building security for minors' data. Adtech firms and ad-funded platforms lose the revenue from individually targeted advertising to users under 17. Indirectly, users may see more generic ads or more paywalls on free services that relied on targeted ads to minors.

drawbacks.text: The teen protections do not require platforms to verify users' ages: the bill expressly says an operator need not implement age gating or age verification, so the ban on targeted ads applies only when the platform knows or should know a user is under 17, and much targeting of teens could continue where age is unknown.
FTC guidance on how to judge a platform's knowledge is non-binding: it confers no rights and cannot be the basis of an enforcement action unless the underlying practice violates the act itself.
The bill requires a Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis of the impact on small entities, acknowledging that compliance costs fall on small websites and app makers as well as large platforms.

Operators acting under written agreements with schools may collect children's and teens' personal information without parental consent, provided it is limited to educational purposes — a carve-out that routes student data through commercial operators with the school, rather than the parent, as the consenting party.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are real and popular: no individually targeted ads to minors, deletion rights, data-minimization, and security requirements are meaningful limits on an adtech model built on profiling young users. But the design has a known weakness — without any age-verification duty, enforcement against platforms that quietly profile teens depends on proving the platform knew the user's age. The school-consent carve-out also leaves a significant channel of student data collection outside parental control. Net effect: a genuine improvement over the 1998 law, with gaps an honest supporter should acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate with a unanimous vote, but since arriving in the House on March 16, 2026 it has been held at the desk — House leaders have not brought it up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Markey on March 4, 2025 and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.

On June 25, 2025 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments; it was formally reported by Senator Cruz, the committee chair, with amendments and a written report on January 27, 2026, and placed on the Senate calendar.
The Senate passed the bill with amendments by unanimous consent on March 5, 2026.

The Senate-passed text covers teens 13 through 16, bans individual-specific advertising to children and teens based on their personal information, and adds deletion, correction, and access rights plus security requirements.
The House received the bill on March 16, 2026 and held it at the desk; no committee referral or floor action has followed.
The bill has 21 cosponsors: 13 Democrats, 7 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, nothing has changed: platforms and adtech firms can continue collecting and monetizing the data of users under 17 exactly as before, while the bill waits at the House desk. The pending outcome favors any business whose revenue depends on targeted advertising to minors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's Democratic sponsor drew 7 Republican and 1 Independent cosponsors, the Republican committee chair reported it favorably, and the Senate passed it by unanimous consent with no recorded opposition; the only obstacle so far is inaction in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill bans building and using individual profiles of children and teens to target them with ads, eliminating ad revenue derived from profiling users under 17. Adtech's interest in keeping that targeting runs directly against the privacy protections ordinary families would gain.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and consumer apps
industries.note: Platforms must honor deletion and correction requests from teens, minimize data collected, secure it, and give notice before storing it abroad — compliance costs that hit hardest at ad-supported free services. The carve-out from age-verification duties softens but does not eliminate the burden.

The bill lets operators acting under written school agreements collect student personal information without parental consent, as long as it is limited to educational purposes — locking in the edtech industry's role as the collector of classroom data, with the school rather than the parent authorizing it, while giving parents notice and review rights.

analysis.trajectory: This is the second Congress running for an updated children's online privacy law to pass the Senate and then stall in the House. The bill sits at the House desk with no committee referral; unless House leadership schedules a vote or it is attached to a larger package, the most likely path is that it sits until the 119th Congress ends and expires. Its unanimous Senate passage and bipartisan cosponsorship keep it a candidate for floor action if leadership chooses.
